notes.front: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled airspace?
notes.back: Controlled airspace (Classes A to E) is where air traffic control (ATC) service is provided; uncontrolled airspace (Class G) is everything else.
notes.explanation: The class tells a remote pilot whether ATC authorisation is needed before flying there.
notes.example: Like roads with and without traffic police: in controlled airspace, controllers manage traffic; in Class G, air traffic control does not manage traffic.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Controlled Airspace”

notes.front: What is a statute mile (SM)?
notes.back: The mile used for visibility in US weather reports, abbreviated SM; it is shorter than the nautical mile used on aviation charts.
notes.explanation: Visibility in US weather reports is given in statute miles, the same unit as part 107’s 3-statute-mile visibility minimum (§ 107.51).
notes.example: ‘5SM’ in a weather report is a prevailing visibility of 5 statute miles.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 16, “Sectional Charts”; AIM para. 7-1-28 (visibility in statute miles); 14 CFR § 107.51(c)

notes.front: What is a nautical mile (NM)?
notes.back: A unit of distance longer than a statute mile: 6.86 nautical miles is about 8 statute miles.
notes.explanation: 14 CFR § 1.2 abbreviates nautical mile as NM. Chart scales and many airspace dimensions use it.
notes.example: On a 1:500,000 sectional, one inch is 6.86 NM, roughly 8 SM.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 16, “Sectional Charts”; 14 CFR § 1.2 Abbreviations and symbols

notes.front: What are visual flight rules (VFR)?
notes.back: Flight rules for weather good enough to see and avoid other aircraft; VFR pilots must keep to minimum visibility and cloud-distance rules.
notes.explanation: VFR pilots are responsible for seeing and avoiding other traffic (14 CFR 91.113) and must meet basic VFR weather minimums (91.155); § 1.2 abbreviates the rules VFR.
notes.example: The PHAK warns that continuing VFR flight into instrument conditions can lead to spatial disorientation or collision with the ground.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 1 (14 CFR part 91) and ch. 2; 14 CFR §§ 1.1, 1.2; AIM para. 4-3-22 (VFR weather minimums; see-and-avoid)

notes.front: What are instrument flight rules (IFR)?
notes.back: Flight rules that let aircraft fly by instruments in weather below VFR minimums (“IFR conditions”), with ATC separating them.
notes.explanation: 14 CFR § 1.1 defines “IFR conditions” as weather below the minimum for flight under VFR; ATC provides separation for aircraft on IFR clearances.
notes.example: The PHAK: “Unless otherwise authorized, all operation in Class A airspace is conducted under instrument flight rules (IFR).”
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 15, “Class A Airspace”; 14 CFR §§ 1.1, 1.2

notes.front: What is a flight level (FL)?
notes.back: A level of constant atmospheric pressure, stated in hundreds of feet: flight level 250 is an altimeter reading of 25,000 feet.
notes.explanation: In NOTAMs, heights of 18,000 feet and above are given as flight levels rather than in feet MSL.
notes.example: A NOTAM gives 18,000 feet as flight level 180, written with FL in front.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 1.1 General definitions (“Flight level”); Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 1, “Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs)”

notes.front: What is Class A airspace?
notes.back: Airspace from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL 600, where flight is normally under instrument flight rules.
notes.explanation: It lies far above any part 107 operation, but completes the set of classes.
notes.example: The layer used by airliners cruising at 35,000 feet.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 15, p. 15-2, “Class A Airspace”

notes.front: What is Class B airspace?
notes.back: Airspace from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL around the busiest airports, shaped in layers like an upside-down wedding cake.
notes.explanation: Each Class B area is individually tailored; a remote pilot needs ATC authorisation to fly in it.
notes.example: The airspace around a major hub such as a big-city international airport.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class B Airspace”

notes.front: What is Class C airspace?
notes.back: Airspace from the surface to 4,000 feet above airport elevation around busy towered airports with radar approach control.
notes.explanation: It usually has a 5 NM-radius surface area and a 10 NM outer shelf from 1,200 to 4,000 feet above the airport.
notes.example: A medium-sized regional airport with its own radar approach control.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class C Airspace”

notes.front: What is Class D airspace?
notes.back: Airspace from the surface to 2,500 feet above airport elevation around airports with an operational control tower.
notes.explanation: Each Class D area is tailored to the airport; a remote pilot needs ATC authorisation to fly in it.
notes.example: A smaller towered airfield used by flight schools and business jets.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class D Airspace”

notes.front: What is Class E airspace?
notes.back: Controlled airspace that is not Class A, B, C or D; it covers much of the United States.
notes.explanation: Its floor is commonly 1,200 or 700 feet AGL or the surface, and it usually extends up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL.
notes.example: The controlled airspace above open countryside, beginning 1,200 feet above the ground.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class E Airspace”

notes.front: What is Class G airspace?
notes.back: Uncontrolled airspace: from the surface up to the base of the overlying Class E airspace.
notes.explanation: A remote pilot does not need ATC authorisation to operate in Class G.
notes.example: Below a Class E floor of 700 feet AGL, a drone at 300 feet over a field is in Class G.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class G Airspace”

image.alt: FAA airspace profile: Class A (red) from 18,000 feet MSL to FL 600; below it Class E, with Class G pink areas at the surface under Class E floors of 700 or 1,200 feet AGL (and up to 14,500 feet MSL in the far left column); a three-tier yellow Class B; a two-tier green Class C; and an orange Class D cylinder around a towered airport.
image.credit: FAA, Remote Pilot – Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, Figure 2-1 (Airspace profile)

notes.front: Where does § 107.41 require prior ATC authorisation?
notes.back: In Class B, C or D airspace, and within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E designated for an airport.
notes.explanation: Elsewhere in Class E, and in Class G, no authorisation is needed.
notes.example: A roof inspection 2 miles from a towered airport, inside its Class D, needs authorisation first.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.41 Operation in certain airspace (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What do UAS Facility Maps show?
notes.back: The pre-approved altitudes at which authorisations can be granted in controlled airspace near airports.
notes.explanation: Requests at or below these altitudes can be approved quickly; higher requests need further coordination.
notes.example: A map grid square near an airport marked “100” means authorisation up to 100 feet can be pre-approved there.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: What is LAANC?
notes.back: The Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability: near-real-time airspace authorisations at UAS Facility Map altitudes, through FAA-approved service suppliers.
notes.explanation: Pilots request through desktop or mobile apps from FAA-approved UAS Service Suppliers.
notes.example: A pilot opens an approved app at the site, asks for 100 feet in Class D, and gets approval within moments.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: What is FAADroneZone used for in airspace authorisation?
notes.back: Requesting authorisations for airports not served by LAANC, processed manually at FAA Air Traffic Service Centers.
notes.explanation: It can be used at LAANC airports too, but approvals are not near-real-time.
notes.example: For an airport without LAANC, the pilot files a request online well ahead.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: What is a warning area?
notes.back: Airspace extending from 3 NM outward from the US coast, containing activity that may be hazardous to non-participating aircraft.
notes.explanation: It is like a restricted area, but the US government does not have sole jurisdiction over it.
notes.example: W-237 off the coast, charted with a “W” and a number.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Warning Areas”

notes.front: What is a military operation area (MOA)?
notes.back: Airspace with defined limits set up to separate certain military training activities from IFR traffic.
notes.explanation: MOAs are named, not numbered, and details are on the back of sectional charts.
notes.example: The Camden Ridge MOA is an example.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Military Operation Areas (MOAs)”

notes.front: What is an alert area?
notes.back: Airspace charted with “A” and a number, warning of a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity.
notes.explanation: Pilots should exercise caution; everyone in it, participating or not, shares responsibility for collision avoidance.
notes.example: A-211, the Study Guide’s example, charted with an “A” and a number like a restricted area’s “R”.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Alert Areas”

notes.front: What is a controlled firing area (CFA)?
notes.back: Airspace containing hazardous activities that are suspended when a spotter aircraft, radar or ground lookout sees an aircraft approaching.
notes.explanation: CFAs are not charted because they do not make non-participating aircraft change course.
notes.example: Blasting that stops whenever a lookout reports an aircraft nearby.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Controlled Firing Areas (CFAs)”

notes.front: What is a military training route (MTR)?
notes.back: A route used by military aircraft to practise tactical flying, usually below 10,000 feet MSL at over 250 knots, marked IR or VR.
notes.explanation: IR routes are flown under instrument rules and VR routes under visual rules.
notes.example: Charted as, e.g., VR1207 or IR206: the letters give the flight rules, the digits the route number.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Military Training Routes (MTRs)”

notes.front: What is a terminal radar service area (TRSA)?
notes.back: An area where pilots who choose to call ATC get extra radar help to keep clear of other aircraft; participation is voluntary.
notes.explanation: The primary airport inside a TRSA is Class D; the rest normally overlies Class E.
notes.example: Charted with a solid black line and altitudes for each segment.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Terminal Radar Service Areas (TRSAs)”

notes.front: What is a national security area (NSA)?
notes.back: Airspace over ground facilities needing extra security, which pilots are asked to avoid voluntarily.
notes.explanation: Flight in an NSA may be temporarily prohibited under 14 CFR part 99, announced by NOTAM.
notes.example: Airspace over a sensitive government facility, charted as an NSA.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “National Security Areas (NSAs)”

notes.front: What are the vertical limits of Class B airspace, generally?
notes.back: From the surface to 10,000 feet MSL.
notes.explanation: Its layers are individually tailored and contain all published instrument procedures.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class B Airspace”

notes.front: What are the usual dimensions of Class C airspace?
notes.back: A 5 NM-radius surface area and a 10 NM-radius shelf from 1,200 to 4,000 feet above airport elevation.
notes.explanation: The whole area is charted in MSL, although defined relative to airport elevation.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class C Airspace”

notes.front: Class D airspace generally extends from the surface to {{c1::2,500 feet}} above the airport elevation.
notes.explanation: Class D exists only around airports with an operational control tower.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class D Airspace”

notes.front: What are the commonest floors of Class E airspace?
notes.back: In most areas 1,200 feet AGL; in many others the surface or 700 feet AGL.
notes.explanation: Some Class E begins at a charted MSL altitude instead.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class E Airspace”

notes.front: How high does Class E airspace typically extend, and where else is it found?
notes.back: Up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL; all airspace above FL 600 is also Class E.
notes.explanation: Where charts show no Class E base, it begins at 14,500 feet MSL.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class E Airspace”

notes.front: Does a remote pilot usually need ATC authorisation to fly in Class E airspace?
notes.back: In most cases, no; only within the surface area of Class E designated for an airport.
notes.explanation: Section 107.41 names only that part of Class E.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class E Airspace”

notes.front: Under what flight rules is Class A airspace normally used?
notes.back: Instrument flight rules (IFR), unless otherwise authorised.
notes.explanation: Class A starts at 18,000 feet MSL, far above part 107 flights.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 15, p. 15-2, “Class A Airspace”

notes.front: Is any notice or authorisation needed to fly near an airport outside controlled airspace?
notes.back: No, but the remote PIC must avoid traffic patterns and approach corridors and not interfere with airport operations.
notes.explanation: Authorisation is tied to the airspace class, not simply to being near an airport.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.10.1

notes.front: How far in advance may a LAANC authorisation request be submitted?
notes.back: Up to 90 days before the planned flight.
notes.explanation: Requests at or below UAS Facility Map altitudes are usually approved in near-real time.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: Through LAANC, how can a pilot fly above the UAS Facility Map altitude?
notes.back: By a further-coordination request, reviewed by an Air Traffic Manager, for flight under 400 feet, submitted at least 72 hours ahead.
notes.explanation: Denied requests may come with guidance so the pilot can adjust and resubmit.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: Are FAADroneZone airspace authorisations available for night operations?
notes.back: Yes; FAADroneZone authorisations are available for both day and night operations.
notes.explanation: Requests above UAS Facility Map altitudes but at or below 400 feet are coordinated with the air traffic facility.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: How are prohibited and restricted areas identified on charts?
notes.back: “P” or “R” followed by a number, e.g. P-40 or R-4401.
notes.explanation: Details of restricted areas are on the back of the chart.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Prohibited Areas; Restricted Areas”

notes.front: Does § 107.45 require permission to fly in a MOA, warning area or alert area?
notes.back: No; § 107.45 requires permission only for prohibited or restricted areas.
notes.explanation: Caution is still needed: these areas can hold fast military or training traffic.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.45 Operation in prohibited or restricted areas (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: What does the number of digits in an MTR identifier tell you?
notes.back: Four digits: no segment above 1,500 feet AGL. Three digits: one or more segments above 1,500 feet AGL.
notes.explanation: Four-digit routes are flown entirely at low level, where drones operate.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Military Training Routes (MTRs)”

notes.front: Which FAA website can a pilot check for TFRs in the area of flight?
notes.back: tfr.faa.gov.
notes.explanation: Being aware of TFRs is the pilot’s responsibility; incursions have led to certificate suspensions.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFR)”

notes.front: Where can a remote pilot obtain NOTAMs?
notes.back: From the Federal NOTAM System (FNS) NOTAM Search website, from Flight Service (the FAA’s pilot briefing service, e.g. 1800wxbrief.com), or private vendors.
notes.explanation: The AC points remote pilots to 1800wxbrief.com for NOTAMs and TFRs.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 5-1-1 and 5-1-2, “Preflight Preparation; Follow IFR Procedures Even When Operating VFR”

notes.front: How far before an activity may a NOTAM be disseminated, and when is it cancelled?
notes.back: Up to 7 days before; it is cancelled when the information is charted or the condition returns to normal.
notes.explanation: NOTAMs carry temporary information or information awaiting publication.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 5-1-3, “Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) System”

notes.front: Where are parachute jump aircraft operations published?
notes.back: In the Chart Supplement; frequently used sites are also shown on sectional charts.
notes.explanation: Parachute jump areas are one of the “other airspace areas”.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Parachute Jump Aircraft Operations”

notes.front: What are published VFR routes for?
notes.back: Transitioning around, under or through complex airspace, such as a Class B VFR transition route.
notes.explanation: They are generally found on VFR terminal area planning charts.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Published VFR Routes”

notes.front: What is local airport advisory (LAA)?
notes.back: A radio advisory from a Flight Service station at the landing airport, on its own frequency or the tower frequency when the tower is closed.
notes.explanation: It includes local advisories and automated weather reporting.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Local Airport Advisory (LAA)”

notes.front: What is the primary purpose of the air traffic control system?
notes.back: To prevent collisions between aircraft in the system, and to organise and expedite the flow of traffic.
notes.explanation: Additional services depend on factors such as traffic volume and controller workload.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Air Traffic Control and the National Airspace System”

notes.front: How far can guy wires extend from an antenna tower, and how far away should pilots stay?
notes.back: About 1,500 feet horizontally; stay at least 2,000 feet horizontally from skeletal structures.
notes.explanation: Guy wires are hard to see in good weather and can be invisible at dusk or in poor visibility.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 11, “Antenna Towers”

notes.front: How tall are many radio and TV antenna towers?
notes.back: Many exceed 1,000 feet AGL, and some exceed 2,000 feet AGL.
notes.explanation: New towers may not appear on current charts.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-4, “Obstructions To Flight”

notes.front: Why is flight at or below 200 feet AGL especially exposed to unseen obstructions?
notes.back: Many power lines and antenna towers there are not marked, lit or charted as obstructions.
notes.explanation: Lines under 200 feet AGL often need no FAA notice, so pilots must stay vigilant.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-4, “Obstructions To Flight”

notes.front: Where are overhead wires commonly found, and how may they be marked?
notes.back: Across runway approaches, rivers, lakes, gorges, highways and railways; sometimes with spherical markers, which may be lit.
notes.explanation: Wires may be virtually impossible to see under certain conditions.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-4, “Obstructions To Flight”

notes.front: What are the three types of obstruction lighting?
notes.back: Red lights (with orange-and-white paint by day); high-intensity white lights; and dual lighting combining red at night with white by day.
notes.explanation: Obstructions are lit or marked to be seen both day and night.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 14, p. 14-19, “Obstruction Lights”

notes.front: When must manned aircraft show position lights?
notes.back: From sunset to sunrise, on the surface and in flight.
notes.explanation: Aircraft with anti-collision systems must also run them day and night, unless in bad weather the pilot decides their light output would be a hazard.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 4-3-24, “Use of Aircraft Lights”

notes.front: What does a manned aircraft’s anti-collision light system look like?
notes.back: One or more rotating beacons and/or strobe lights, coloured red or white.
notes.explanation: Many aircraft have both a rotating beacon and strobes.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 4-3-24, “Use of Aircraft Lights”

notes.front: At night, may a remote pilot rely on the anti-collision light and control-station telemetry to meet VLOS?
notes.back: No. Neither, alone or combined, satisfies § 107.31.
notes.explanation: The remote PIC may need to restrict the operational area at night to keep VLOS.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.9.3, VLOS at Night

notes.front: Before a twilight or night flight, what should the remote PIC check about the anti-collision lights?
notes.back: That they work properly, and whether their power use shortens the flight.
notes.explanation: There must be enough power to keep the lights on and reach a normal landing.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.11.1, Prior to Flight

notes.front: Which general aviation accident causal factor does the AIM list first?
notes.back: Inadequate preflight preparation and/or planning.
notes.explanation: The AIM lists the 10 most frequent pilot-in-command causal factors, including failure to see and avoid objects.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::failure to obtain and/or maintain flying speed}}.
notes.explanation: That is, failing to keep enough speed to stay airborne. The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::failure to maintain direction control}}.
notes.explanation: The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::improper level off}}.
notes.explanation: The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: Which AIM accident causal factor most directly concerns obstacles?
notes.back: Failure to see and avoid objects or obstructions.
notes.explanation: Misjudgment of distance and speed is another factor on the same list.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::mismanagement of fuel}}.
notes.explanation: The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::improper inflight decisions or planning}}.
notes.explanation: The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::misjudgment of distance and speed}}.
notes.explanation: The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::selection of unsuitable terrain}}.
notes.explanation: The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: One of the AIM’s 10 most frequent causal factors in general aviation accidents involving the pilot in command: {{c1::improper operation of flight controls}}.
notes.explanation: The AIM says this list stays fairly stable, which shows why pilots need continued refresher training.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-1, “Accident Causal Factors”

notes.front: Why should pilots avoid flying beneath unmanned free balloons?
notes.back: Suspended payloads or trailing wire antennas below them may be invisible until very close.
notes.explanation: The AIM advises staying well clear of such balloons and reporting sightings.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-5, “Avoid Flight Beneath Unmanned Balloons”

notes.front: Why is an emergency airborne inspection of another aircraft hazardous?
notes.back: It means flying very close to the other aircraft, usually without training or time to plan, under stress.
notes.explanation: The pilot in the best position to assess the situation should coordinate it.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-11, “Emergency Airborne Inspection of Other Aircraft”

notes.front: What causes precipitation static (P-static)?
notes.back: Charge built up on an aircraft flying through particles such as rain, snow or dust, discharged from its extremities.
notes.explanation: It can cause radio noise, loss of communications and erratic instrument readings.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-12, “Precipitation Static”

notes.front: To whom should pilots report a laser illumination?
notes.back: To the air traffic control facility or tower you are in contact with, or to Flight Service, as soon as possible.
notes.explanation: Lasers can impair vision temporarily miles away and cause permanent eye damage.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-13, “Laser Operations and Reporting Illumination of Aircraft”

notes.front: How high can exhaust plume turbulence extend, and how should pilots avoid it?
notes.back: Over 1,000 feet above the top of the stack or cooling tower; fly on the upwind side.
notes.explanation: Effects are worst in calm, cold, stable air; invisible plumes can still be active.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-16, “Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes”

notes.front: Over farmland, Class E starts at 700 feet AGL. A drone flies at 350 feet AGL there. Which class, and is authorisation needed?
notes.back: Class G; no ATC authorisation is needed.
notes.explanation: Class G extends from the surface up to the base of the overlying Class E.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class G Airspace”

notes.front: A site lies 3 miles from an airport with an operating control tower, inside the airspace from the surface to 2,500 feet above it. Which class, and what is needed?
notes.back: Class D; prior ATC authorisation is needed.
notes.explanation: Class D surrounds airports with an operational control tower.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.41 Operation in certain airspace (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: A site lies inside the Class E surface area designated for a non-towered airport. Is authorisation needed?
notes.back: Yes. The surface area of Class E designated for an airport needs prior ATC authorisation.
notes.choices:
A) No, Class E never needs authorisation
B) Yes
C) Only if the airport has a tower
notes.choicesExplained: A: § 107.41 names the Class E surface area for an airport. C: a towered airport usually means Class D; the Class E surface-area rule applies regardless.
notes.explanation: Class E away from an airport’s surface area does not.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.41 Operation in certain airspace (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: Seven NM from a Class C airport, over terrain level with it, a drone flies at 300 feet AGL. Is Class C authorisation needed?
notes.back: No. The outer shelf starts 1,200 feet above airport elevation, so the drone is below Class C.
notes.explanation: Between 5 and 10 NM, Class C does not reach the surface.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class C Airspace”

notes.front: An airport’s airspace has several stacked tiers and rises to 10,000 feet MSL. Which class is it?
notes.back: Class B.
notes.explanation: Class C tops out at 4,000 feet above the airport; Class B reaches 10,000 feet MSL in layers.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class B Airspace”

notes.front: The UAS Facility Map shows 100 feet, but the job needs 300 feet. How can the pilot use LAANC?
notes.back: Submit a further-coordination request at least 72 hours before the flight; it goes to an Air Traffic Manager.
notes.explanation: Near-real-time approval applies only at or below the map altitude.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: A job lies in Class D at an airport not served by LAANC. How does the pilot get authorisation?
notes.back: Apply through FAADroneZone; FAA Air Traffic Service Centers process it manually.
notes.explanation: FAADroneZone approvals are not near-real-time, so apply early.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: A survey site lies under VR1207. What does the identifier tell the remote pilot?
notes.back: A visual-rules military route with no segment above 1,500 feet AGL: fast, low-level traffic.
notes.explanation: Four digits mean the whole route is at or below 1,500 feet AGL.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Military Training Routes (MTRs)”

notes.front: Which special use airspace is described: charted “A-211”; named “Camden Ridge”; begins 3 NM offshore?
notes.back: Alert area; military operation area; warning area.
notes.explanation: Alert areas use “A” and a number, MOAs are named, and warning areas start 3 NM from the coast.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Special Use Airspace”

notes.front: Why will a remote pilot not find a controlled firing area on a sectional chart?
notes.back: CFAs are not charted: their activity stops when an aircraft approaches, so no one needs to reroute.
notes.explanation: This is what sets CFAs apart from other special use airspace.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Controlled Firing Areas (CFAs)”

notes.front: A drone must pass a 1,200-foot TV mast supported by guy wires. What horizontal distance does FAA guidance advise?
notes.back: At least 2,000 feet from the mast, because guy wires can extend about 1,500 feet out.
notes.explanation: Guy wires are very hard to see and may be invisible at dusk.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 11, “Antenna Towers”

notes.front: A chimney flashes bright white by day and shows red beacons and steady red lights at night. Which obstruction lighting is this?
notes.back: Dual lighting.
notes.explanation: Dual lighting combines red lights at night with high-intensity white lights by day.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 14, p. 14-19, “Obstruction Lights”

notes.front: At night the drone becomes a single flashing dot; the pilot tracks it by the light and the map on the controller. Is VLOS met?
notes.back: No. The pilot cannot rely solely on the anti-collision light and telemetry; they must see its location, attitude, altitude and direction.
notes.explanation: At night the remote PIC may need to shrink the operating area.
notes.source: AC 107-2A, Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (2021), ¶5.9.3, VLOS at Night

notes.front: At dusk a remote pilot sees steady coloured lights and a flashing red beacon moving across the sky. What is it likely to be?
notes.back: A manned aircraft showing position lights and a rotating beacon or strobe anti-collision light.
notes.explanation: Position lights are shown from sunset to sunrise; anti-collision lights are red or white.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 4-3-24, “Use of Aircraft Lights”

notes.front: A power station stack is near the survey route on a calm, cold morning. How does the AIM advise avoiding the plume?
notes.back: Fly on the upwind side of the stack and stay clear, even if no plume is visible.
notes.explanation: Plume effects can reach over 1,000 feet above the stack.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual (Change 3, 9 July 2026), para 7-6-16, “Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes”

notes.front: How does the § 107.41 airspace authorisation differ from the § 107.45 permission?
notes.back: § 107.41: authorisation from ATC for Class B, C, D or airport surface-area Class E. § 107.45: permission from the using or controlling agency.
notes.explanation: Different airspace, different authority.
notes.contrast: Controlled airspace: ATC. Prohibited/restricted areas: the using or controlling agency.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.45 Operation in prohibited or restricted areas (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: How do Class C and Class D airspace differ in height?
notes.back: Class C: surface to 4,000 feet above airport elevation, with an outer shelf. Class D: surface to 2,500 feet above airport elevation.
notes.explanation: Both surround towered airports and need ATC authorisation for part 107 flight.
notes.contrast: C: 4,000 feet and a shelf. D: 2,500 feet, shaped individually for each airport.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Class C Airspace; Class D Airspace”

notes.front: What is the key part 107 difference between a MOA and a restricted area?
notes.back: A restricted area needs permission from its using or controlling agency; a MOA needs none under § 107.45, only caution.
notes.explanation: Restricted areas hold hazards such as live firing; MOAs separate military training from IFR traffic.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.45 Operation in prohibited or restricted areas (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date

notes.front: How does a warning area differ from a restricted area?
notes.back: A warning area lies from 3 NM offshore, where the US government lacks sole jurisdiction; a restricted area lies under US control.
notes.explanation: Both contain activity hazardous to non-participating aircraft.
notes.contrast: Warning: offshore, warns. Restricted: under US jurisdiction, restricts.
notes.source: Remote Pilot – sUAS Study Guide FAA-G-8082-22, ch. 2, “Warning Areas”

notes.front: How do LAANC and FAADroneZone authorisations differ?
notes.back: LAANC gives near-real-time approvals through approved suppliers; FAADroneZone requests are processed manually, not in near-real time.
notes.explanation: FAADroneZone serves airports without LAANC and can also be used where LAANC exists.
notes.contrast: LAANC: automated and fast. FAADroneZone: manual and slower.
notes.source: FAA, Part 107 Airspace Authorizations (web page, last updated 14 September 2026)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA Part 107 Airspace Authorizations page (last updated 14 September 2026)

notes.front: In Class B, manned VFR flight needs 3 statute miles and “clear of clouds”. What does part 107 require there?
notes.back: 3 statute miles flight visibility, and at least 500 feet below and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds, as everywhere.
notes.explanation: Part 107 uses § 107.51 in every class; the manned VFR table is context only.
notes.contrast: Manned VFR minimums vary by class. Part 107 cloud clearance is the same everywhere.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge FAA-H-8083-25C, ch. 15, p. 15-8, “Basic VFR Weather Minimums”

notes.front: What is the part 107 difference between Class E surface area and Class E starting at 700 feet AGL?
notes.back: Class E surface area designated for an airport needs ATC authorisation; under a 700-foot floor, a drone is in Class G and needs none.
notes.explanation: The class at the drone’s actual altitude is what counts.
notes.contrast: E to the surface: authorise. E from 700 feet: the drone is below it, in Class G.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 107.41 Operation in certain airspace (eCFR)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 14 CFR Part 107 as of that date
